summary: The evidence supports a single causal chain: at 14:08 a downstream catalog API cut the per-client rate limit by 35% (E4), producing 429 responses whose requests were retried twice with exponential backoff (E5); that added wait time is what doubled median search latency from 14:10 (E1). The concurrent cache hit-rate drop from 91% to 76% (E2) is a side effect rather than a cause: it was produced by retry traffic carrying a cache-bypass header (E7), the cache service itself was healthy (E3), and requests that never saw a 429 showed no latency increase regardless of cache hit or miss (E6). The intervention at 14:41 closes the loop: restoring the prior rate limit ended the 429 spike and latency normalized about two minutes later (E8), consistent with the recovery at 14:43 (E1). The package does not quantify how much of the latency came from backoff waiting versus extra downstream work, does not say why the rate limit was changed, and does not describe latency at the tail rather than the median.

claims.text: Median search latency doubled from 14:10 and recovered at 14:43.
The downstream catalog API's 35% per-client rate-limit reduction at 14:08 initiated the incident window, two minutes before the latency rise.
The rate-limit reduction caused search requests to receive downstream 429 responses.
Two retries with exponential backoff on 429-affected requests are the proximate mechanism of the added latency.
Exposure to a downstream 429 is what separates slow requests from normal ones; cache outcome is not.
The cache hit-rate decline from 91% to 76% was caused by retry requests setting a cache-bypass header.
The cache hit-rate decline is a downstream symptom of the retry behavior, not a cause of the latency increase.
The cache service was not degraded during the window.
Restoring the previous rate limit at 14:41 removed the 429 spike and latency normalized roughly two minutes later.
The intervention result is a deliberate manipulation of the suspected cause, which strengthens the causal reading beyond mere temporal correlation.
The retry policy acted as an amplifier: it converted a downstream quota change into both a latency cost and additional cache-bypassing load.
The evidence describes only median latency, so the effect on tail latency and on error rates visible to users is not established.

uncertainties.text: How much of the doubled median latency came from backoff wait time versus repeated downstream work or the extra cache-bypassing requests is not separated.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: Per-request latency decomposition showing time spent in backoff sleep, in downstream calls, and in cache lookups, split by retry count.

uncertainties.text: Why the downstream catalog API reduced the per-client rate limit at 14:08 is not stated, so whether it was a deliberate change, an automated response to its own load, or a misconfiguration is unresolved.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: Change record or operator statement from the catalog API team covering the 14:08 and 14:41 rate-limit changes.

uncertainties.text: Why retry requests carry a cache-bypass header is not explained; it may be intentional design or an unintended default.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: The retry client's code or configuration showing where the bypass header is set and the rationale.

uncertainties.text: Whether the extra cache-bypass traffic added measurable load on the cache or the catalog API is unknown; the cache reported normal latency, but downstream impact is not described.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: Request-volume and saturation metrics for the cache and catalog API across the window, split by bypass header.

uncertainties.text: The two-minute lag between the 14:41 restoration and 14:43 normalization is unexplained; it could be in-flight backoff draining, metric aggregation windows, or propagation delay.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: Fine-grained (sub-minute) 429 rate and latency series between 14:41 and 14:43, plus the metric aggregation interval.

uncertainties.text: The share of search traffic that received 429s is not quantified, so the size of the affected population is unknown.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: Counts of search requests with and without a downstream 429 per minute during the window.

uncertainties.text: Tail latency, request failures, and any user-visible errors after retries were exhausted are not reported.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: p95/p99 latency and terminal error rates for search over the same window.

uncertainties.text: Whether this pattern occurred before, or whether the 14:08 change was unprecedented, is not covered by the package.
uncertainties.resolvedBy: Historical 429 and latency data for prior rate-limit changes on the same downstream API.

actions.text: Treat the downstream rate-limit change as the root cause of record and the retry-on-429 policy as the amplifying mechanism; do not open cache-focused remediation.
Remove or condition the cache-bypass header on retries so retried requests can still be served from cache, which decouples hit rate from 429 volume.
Revisit the retry policy for 429 specifically (for example, honor Retry-After, cap concurrency, or shed load) so quota reductions degrade throughput rather than latency.
Establish a change-notification or coordination path with the catalog API owners for per-client rate-limit changes.
Add an alert on downstream 429 rate as a leading indicator, since it preceded the latency signal and was the discriminating variable.
Collect the tail-latency and error-rate data for this window before closing the incident, since only the median is currently described.

counterfactuals.text: Had the per-client rate limit not been reduced at 14:08, no 429 spike would have occurred and median latency would likely have stayed flat.
Had the cache hit rate been held at 91% while 429s and retries continued, latency would likely still have doubled, since non-429 requests were unaffected regardless of cache outcome.
Had retries not used the cache-bypass header, the hit-rate drop would probably not have appeared, while the latency increase would likely have persisted.
Had 429-affected requests failed fast instead of retrying twice with backoff, median latency would likely have risen much less, at the cost of a higher visible error rate.
Had the rate limit been restored earlier than 14:41, recovery would likely have arrived correspondingly earlier, given the roughly two-minute lag observed.
Had the cache service itself degraded, requests without 429s should also have slowed; that was not observed, so a cache-origin explanation is not supported.
